## Overview

::: {.incremental}
1. **GitHub Copilot** — inline suggestions in RStudio
2. **Claude Code** — agentic AI in your project directory
3. **`btw` package** — R session as a live AI tool + token economy

5. **LM Studio** — offline AI on a plane or airgapped server

---

## Why AI for R?

R has a rich ecosystem but:

- Syntax quirks across dialects (base R / tidyverse / data.table)
- Package discovery is hard
- Error messages are cryptic
- Writing boilerplate is tedious

**AI tools make you faster at the parts that aren't the interesting parts.**

::: {.notes}
The goal isn't to replace thinking — it's to reduce friction. You still need to understand the code.
:::

---

# GitHub Copilot {background-color="#1e3a5f" background-image="dec_pic_close_1.jpg" background-opacity="0.15"}

Inline AI code completion inside RStudio

---

## Setting up Copilot in RStudio

```r
# 1. Ensure RStudio >= 2023.09
rstudioapi::versionInfo()$version

# 2. Enable: Tools → Global Options → Copilot → Enable
# 3. Sign in with GitHub account (free for students/researchers)
```

**What Copilot does well:**

- Completes function calls with correct argument names
- Suggests the next line based on context
- Generates boilerplate (ggplot themes, model formulas)

**What it doesn't do:**

- Understand your actual data structure
- React to errors and iterate
- Browse files in your project

---

## Copilot in action

Start typing and Copilot fills in the rest:

```r
# Read and summarise a CSV, grouping by species
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>         # ← Copilot suggests this
  summarise(
    n = n(),                   # ← and this
    mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

::: {.callout-tip}
**Tab** accepts. **Alt+]** cycles through alternatives. **Esc** rejects.
:::

---

## Copilot limits

```r
# Copilot doesn't know your column names
my_dataset |>
  group_by(kolumn_nimetus_eesti_keeles) |>  # guesses, often wrong
  ...

# It also can't react to this:
# Error in group_by(): Column `kolumn_nimetus_eesti_keeles` not found
```

This is where **agentic AI** wins.

---

# Claude Code {background-color="#2d1b69" background-image="dec_pic_middle1.jpg" background-opacity="0.15"}

Agentic AI that reads, writes, and runs — in your project directory

---

## What is "agentic" AI?

A regular LLM chat:

> You paste code → AI replies → you paste back → repeat

An **agent**:

> AI reads your files → edits them → runs commands → checks output → iterates

Claude Code is a CLI tool you run **inside your R project directory**.

```bash
# Install (requires Node.js)
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

# Run inside your project
cd ~/Documents/R/my-project
claude
```

---

## Claude Code — what it can do

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Reads:**

- All files in your project
- Git history
- R scripts, QMDs, CSVs

**Writes:**

- Edits files directly
- Creates new files
- Runs bash/R commands
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Understands:**

- Your project structure
- Package dependencies
- Error messages from R
- What changed since last commit
:::
:::

---

## Working in the same directory

```
my-project/
├── data/
│   └── measurements.csv    # Claude can read this
├── analysis.R               # Claude can edit this
├── report.qmd               # Claude can render this
└── README.md                # Claude maintains this
```

Claude sees **the same files you do**. No copy-pasting. No context switching.

::: {.callout-important}
Claude Code runs with your filesystem permissions. Always `git commit` before a session so you can roll back.
:::

---

## Good prompts for Claude Code

```
# Name the files and describe the output explicitly
> Analyse data/sales.csv and write a ggplot bar chart
  of monthly totals to plots/monthly.png

# Ask it to explain before touching anything
> Before changing anything, explain what's wrong
  with the join in analysis.R lines 55–60

# Chain tasks in one prompt
> Fix the bug, re-render report.qmd, show me the diff
```

---

# `btw` package {background-color="#1a4731" background-image="dec_pic_open1.jpg" background-opacity="0.12"}

Giving AI precise context about your R session — and connecting R as an MCP server

---

## The problem `btw` solves

When you ask an LLM about R code, it doesn't know:

- What packages you have installed
- What version of R you're running
- What objects are in your environment
- What your data actually looks like

`btw` snapshots your session and formats it for an LLM.

```r
# Install
install.packages("btw")
# or dev version:
pak::pak("posit-dev/btw")

library(btw)
```

---

## Setting up the API key

`btw` connects to Claude (Anthropic API) to power its MCP tools.

**Step 1 — Get a key:** [console.anthropic.com](https://console.anthropic.com) → API Keys → Create

**Step 2 — Add to R environment** (persists across sessions):

```r
# Opens ~/.Renviron in your editor
usethis::edit_r_environ()
```

Add this line and save, then **restart R**:

```sh
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-api03-YOUR-KEY-HERE
```

**Step 3 — Verify:**

```r
Sys.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY")  # should not be ""
```

::: {.callout-warning}
Never paste API keys into scripts or commit them to git. `.Renviron` lives in your home directory and is git-ignored by default.
:::

---

## `btw()` — copy session context

```r
library(btw)
library(palmerpenguins)

penguins_clean <- penguins |> tidyr::drop_na()

# Copies a rich session description to clipboard
btw(penguins_clean)
```

Paste into Claude.ai, ChatGPT, or Copilot Chat — it instantly knows:

- Column names and types
- Sample values
- Your R version and loaded packages

---

## What `btw()` produces

````
## Data frame: penguins_clean (333 × 8)

| Column         | Type   | Example values              |
|----------------|--------|-----------------------------|
| species        | factor | Adelie, Gentoo, Chinstrap   |
| island         | factor | Torgersen, Biscoe, Dream    |
| bill_length_mm | dbl    | 39.1, 39.5, 40.3            |
| body_mass_g    | int    | 3750, 3800, 3250            |
...

## Session info
R 4.5.0 · dplyr 1.1.4 · ggplot2 3.5.1
````

Now the LLM writes **correct** column names, not guesses.

---

## R as an MCP server

**MCP = Model Context Protocol** — a standard for giving AI agents live tools.

`btw` exposes your **running R session** as an MCP server so Claude Code can:

- Inspect objects in your environment as they are right now
- Run R code and receive results
- Read help pages and vignettes on demand
- Query installed packages and CRAN

---

## Setting up R as MCP for Claude Code

**Step 1 — Start the btw MCP server in R:**

```r
btw::btw_app()   # starts MCP server in background
```

**Step 2 — Tell Claude Code where to find it.**

Edit `~/.claude/settings.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "r-btw": {
      "command": "Rscript",
      "args": ["-e", "btw::btw_app()"],
      "env": {
        "ANTHROPIC_API_KEY": "${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

**Step 3 — Restart Claude Code.** It auto-connects.

---

## What you can now ask Claude Code

With R connected as MCP:

```
> What data frames are currently in my R environment?

> Describe the structure of the `survey_data` object

> What does the REML argument in lme4::lmer do?

> My session has palmerpenguins loaded — fit a mixed
  model of bill length by species + island
```

Claude calls your **live R session** for answers — no copy-paste.

---

## Saving tokens — why it matters

LLM APIs charge per token. A sloppy workflow burns money fast:

| Habit | Approx tokens |
|---|---|
| `btw()` — whole environment | 2,000–10,000 |
| `btw(my_df)` — one data frame | 200–600 |
| Pasting entire help page | 3,000–8,000 |
| `btw_tool_docs_help_page("pkg","fn")` | 400–1,200 |
| Re-explaining project context every session | 500–2,000 |
| `CLAUDE.md` project file (read once) | 200–500 |

**Rule: describe only what the model needs to answer this specific question.**

---

## Token-saving techniques with btw

```r
# BAD — sends your entire environment
btw()

# GOOD — send only what's needed
btw(bw_data)

# BETTER — limit to a sample
btw(head(bw_data, 10))

# Targeted help lookup (doesn't paste the whole page)
btw_tool_docs_help_page("dplyr", "group_by")

# Check only what's installed, not full session
btw_tool_sessioninfo_is_package_installed("sf")
```

---

## CLAUDE.md — your project memory

Create a `CLAUDE.md` file in your project root. Claude Code reads it at every session start — **you never re-explain your project**.

```markdown
# CLAUDE.md

## Project
EEA bathing water quality analysis, 1990–2024.
Main data: data/bw_assessment_eea_datahub_1990_2024_data.csv (672k rows)

## Key columns
- `countryCode`: ISO2 country code
- `season`: year of assessment
- `quality`: EEA quality class (Excellent / Good / Sufficient / Poor)
- `bathingWaterType`: coastalBathingWater | inlandBathingWater

## Conventions
- Use dplyr + ggplot2
- Save all plots to plots/ as PNG at 300 dpi
- All analysis scripts source data/load_data.R first
```

Zero tokens spent re-orienting the agent.

---

## `btw` — other useful functions

```r
# Describe one data frame (most common use)
btw(my_df)

# Targeted function documentation
btw_tool_docs_help_page("lme4", "lmer")

# All vignettes for a package
btw_tool_docs_available_vignettes("sf")

# What's in my environment right now?
btw_tool_env_describe_environment()

# CRAN page and metadata for a package
btw_tool_cran_package("ggplot2")

# Search CRAN by topic
btw_tool_cran_search("spatial interpolation")
```

# Quarto Templates {background-color="#4a1942"}

Reusable YAML so you never set up the same slide twice

---

## The YAML repetition problem

Every new presentation you write this from scratch:

```yaml
---
title: "My Talk"
author: "Peeter"           # ← type this every time
institute: "UT / TalTech"  # ← type this every time
format:
  revealjs:
    theme: dark            # ← set this every time
    slide-number: true     # ← set this every time
    self-contained: true   # ← forget this every time
---
```

**Solution:** a project-level `_quarto.yml` that sets defaults once.

---

## `_quarto.yml` — your personal template

```yaml
# _quarto.yml — copy to any new project folder
author:
  - name: "Peeter"
    affiliation: "University of Tartu / TalTech"
    email: "peeter@ut.ee"

format:
  revealjs:
    theme: dark
    highlight-style: github-dark
    slide-number: true
    transition: slide
    self-contained: true
    logo: assets/ut_logo.svg
    footer: "{{< meta author >}} · {{< meta date >}}"
  html:
    toc: true
    embed-resources: true

execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
```

Any `.qmd` in this project inherits everything. New talks need only:

```yaml
---
title: "My New Talk"
date: today
---
```

---

## Live data in slides — weather example

Slides fetch real data at **render time**. No manual updates ever.

```{r}
#| label: weather-demo
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

library(httr2)

resp <- request("https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast") |>
  req_url_query(
    latitude  = 58.38,   # Tartu
    longitude = 26.72,
    current   = "temperature_2m,wind_speed_10m",
    timezone  = "Europe/Tallinn"
  ) |>
  req_perform() |>
  resp_body_json()

temp <- resp$current$temperature_2m
wind <- resp$current$wind_speed_10m
```

Then in slide text:

```markdown
Temperature in Tartu right now: **`{r} temp`°C**, wind `{r} wind` km/h
```

**This title slide already does this** — look at the subtitle line.

---

## Template workflow with AI

```bash
# New talk in 30 seconds
mkdir ~/talks/my-new-talk && cd ~/talks/my-new-talk
cp ~/Documents/R/RaiS/_quarto.yml .
claude
```

```
> Create a 10-slide RevealJS presentation titled
> "Spatial Analysis of Estonian Peatlands".
> My identity and formatting are in _quarto.yml.
> Include: intro, methods, 3 results slides, discussion.
> Add a ggplot2 map example using sf.
```

Claude reads `_quarto.yml`, inherits your name, affiliation, and all formatting. You write zero boilerplate.

# LM Studio {background-color="#2c1810"}

Offline AI — your scripting partner on a plane, in the field, or on an airgapped server

---

## Why run a local LLM?

::: {.incremental}
- **No internet** — airplane, fieldwork, rural server room
- **Privacy** — sensitive data that can't leave your machine
- **No API costs** — unlimited queries once model is downloaded
- **Reproducibility** — pin to a specific model version, forever
:::

---

## LM Studio — what it is

LM Studio is a desktop app + CLI that:

- Downloads models from Hugging Face with one click
- Runs them locally via `llama.cpp` (CPU) or GPU acceleration
- Exposes an **OpenAI-compatible API** on `localhost:1234`
- Ships with `lms` — a full command-line interface

**Download:** [lmstudio.ai](https://lmstudio.ai) — Mac, Windows, Linux

---

## Installing the `lms` CLI

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Mac / Linux:**

```bash
# LM Studio app → Install CLI tools
# Or manually:
export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/.lmstudio/bin"

lms --version
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Windows:**

```powershell
# LM Studio app → Install CLI tools
# (adds to user PATH automatically)

lms --version
```
:::
:::

---

## `lms` — essential commands

```bash
lms server start                          # start the API server
lms ls                                    # list downloaded models
lms get "qwen2.5-coder-7b-instruct"      # download a model
lms load qwen2.5-coder-7b-instruct-q4_k_m  # load into memory
lms chat                                  # interactive terminal chat
lms status                                # check what's running
lms server stop                           # stop the server
```

---

## Choosing your model — by hardware

| Hardware | Recommended model | Size |
|---|---|---|
| CPU only — Linux / Win | `Phi-4-mini` Q4 | ~2.5 GB |
| CPU only — Linux / Win | `Gemma-3-4B-IT` Q4 | ~3 GB |
| 8 GB VRAM — Linux / Win | `Qwen2.5-Coder-7B` Q4 | ~5 GB |
| 16 GB VRAM — Linux / Win | `Qwen2.5-Coder-14B` Q4 | ~10 GB |
| 24 GB VRAM — Linux / Win | `Mistral-Small-22B` Q4 | ~18 GB |
| Mac 8 GB (M-series) | `Phi-4-mini` Q4 | ~2.5 GB |
| Mac 16 GB (M-series) | `Qwen2.5-Coder-7B` Q4 | ~5 GB |
| Mac 32 GB+ (M-series) | `Qwen2.5-Coder-14B` Q4 | ~10 GB |

::: {.callout-note}
Apple Silicon uses unified memory — a 32 GB MacBook handles what a 32 GB VRAM GPU handles.
**Q4_K_M** is the best quality-per-GB quantisation for all platforms.
:::

---

## Step-by-step: CPU only (Linux / Windows)

```bash
# 1. Install LM Studio from lmstudio.ai, then:
lms server start

# 2. Download a small but capable model (~2.5 GB)
lms get "microsoft/phi-4-mini-instruct-gguf"

# 3. Load it
lms load phi-4-mini-instruct-q4_k_m

# 4. Test in terminal
lms chat
# > Write an R function that reads a CSV and returns
# > summary statistics per numeric column

# 5. Confirm the API is up
curl http://localhost:1234/v1/models
```

Total: ~10 min including download.

---

## Step-by-step: NVIDIA GPU (Linux / Windows)

```bash
# 1. Verify CUDA
nvidia-smi

# 2. Install LM Studio — auto-detects CUDA

# 3. Download coder model (~5 GB)
lms get "qwen2.5-coder-7b-instruct-gguf"

# 4. Load — offload all layers to GPU
lms load qwen2.5-coder-7b-instruct-q4_k_m \
  --gpu-layers 999

# 5. Chat or query via API
lms chat

# 6. Monitor GPU while running
watch -n1 nvidia-smi
```

---

## Step-by-step: Mac Apple Silicon

```bash
# 1. Install LM Studio (Apple Silicon native — uses Metal)

# 2. Download
lms get "qwen2.5-coder-7b-instruct-gguf"

# 3. Load (Metal acceleration is automatic)
lms load qwen2.5-coder-7b-instruct-q4_k_m

# 4. Test
lms chat

# 5. Monitor: Activity Monitor → Window → GPU History
```

---

## Using LM Studio with R

LM Studio exposes an OpenAI-compatible API on `localhost:1234`:

```r
library(httr2)

ask_local_llm <- function(prompt, model = "local-model") {
  request("http://localhost:1234/v1/chat/completions") |>
    req_body_json(list(
      model    = model,
      messages = list(list(role = "user", content = prompt))
    )) |>
    req_perform() |>
    resp_body_json() |>
    (\(r) r$choices[[1]]$message$content)()
}

ask_local_llm("Write a dplyr pipeline to count NAs per column")
```

No API key. No internet. No cost per query.

---

## Using LM Studio with Claude Code offline

Point Claude Code at your local server:

```bash
export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:1234/v1
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=local   # any non-empty string works

claude
```

::: {.callout-warning}
Local models are weaker than Claude — great for focused tasks (fix this function, write a plot) but struggle with complex multi-file reasoning. Use offline; switch back when you have internet.
:::

# Practical Exercises {background-color="#3d2b00"}

---

## Exercise 1 — Copilot warm-up (10 min)

In RStudio with Copilot enabled:

1. Open a new R script
2. Write this comment — let Copilot complete the rest:

```r
# Load mtcars, fit a linear model of mpg ~ wt + cyl,
# and plot residuals vs fitted values
```

3. **Tab** to accept, **Esc** to reject, **Alt+]** to see alternatives
4. Run the code — does it actually work?

**Goal:** get comfortable with the accept/reject cycle before trusting it.

---

## Exercise 2 — Claude Code session (20 min)

```bash
mkdir ~/ai-exercise && cd ~/ai-exercise
git init && claude
```

Ask Claude to:

1. Create `data/sample.csv` with student grades (name, subject, score)
2. Write `analysis.R` that reads it and produces a summary table
3. Create a ggplot bar chart → `plots/grades.png`
4. Write a `report.qmd` that includes both

**Inspect each file before accepting. Run `git diff` after each edit. Render the QMD.**

## Exercise 3 — btw + API key (10 min)

```r
# 1. Add your API key
usethis::edit_r_environ()
# ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-api03-...
# Save → restart R

# 2. Verify
Sys.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY")

# 3. Use btw with real data
library(btw)
library(palmerpenguins)
penguins_problem <- penguins
penguins_problem$body_mass_g[sample(nrow(penguins), 20)] <- NA
btw(penguins_problem)   # copies to clipboard
```

Paste into Claude.ai:

> *"Impute missing `body_mass_g` using the median within each species. dplyr."*

## Demo — downloadable table {.scrollable}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
bw_sample |>
  mutate(quality = factor(quality,
           levels = c("Excellent","Good","Sufficient","Poor"))) |>
  datatable(
    extensions = "Buttons",
    options    = list(
      dom        = "Bfrtip",
      buttons    = list(
        list(extend = "csv",   text = "Download CSV"),
        list(extend = "excel", text = "Download Excel")
      ),
      pageLength = 8,
      scrollY    = "340px",
      scrollCollapse = TRUE
    ),
    filter   = "top",
    rownames = FALSE,
    colnames = c("Country","Site","Type","Quality","Season","Lon","Lat")
  ) |>
  formatStyle(
    "quality",
    backgroundColor = styleEqual(
      names(quality_colours), unname(quality_colours)
    ),
    color = "white", fontWeight = "bold"
  )
```

---

## Demo — interactive map

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
pal <- colorFactor(palette = unname(quality_colours),
                   levels  = names(quality_colours))

leaflet(bw_sample) |>
  addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.DarkMatter) |>
  addCircleMarkers(
    lng         = ~lon,
    lat         = ~lat,
    color       = ~pal(quality),
    fillOpacity = 0.85,
    radius      = 9,
    stroke      = FALSE,
    popup       = ~paste0(
      "<b>", site, "</b><br>",
      country, " &middot; ", type, "<br>",
      "<b style='color:", quality_colours[quality], "'>",
      quality, "</b> &middot; ", season
    )
  ) |>
  addLegend("bottomright", pal = pal, values = ~quality,
            title = "Quality", opacity = 0.9)
```

library(btw)

bw <- readr::read_csv("bw_assessment_eea_datahub_1990_2024_data.csv",
                      show_col_types = FALSE)

## Exercise 4 — EEA Data continued

**Step 2 — Filter and explore a country**

```r
# Filter to your country (or Estonia as example)
bw_ee <- bw |>
  filter(countryCode == "EE", season == 2024)

# Ask AI: quality categories in plain English
btw(bw_ee)
```

> *"Summarise the distribution of quality ratings for Estonian bathing waters in 2024. Write dplyr + ggplot2 code."*

## Exercise 4 — Searchable table with download

A large data frame can be made browsable and downloadable:

```r
library(DT)

bw_ee |>
  select(bathingWaterName, bathingWaterType,
         lon, lat, quality, season) |>
  datatable(
    extensions = "Buttons",
    options = list(
      dom       = "Bfrtip",
      buttons   = c("csv", "excel"),
      pageLength = 15
    ),
    filter    = "top",      # per-column filter boxes
    rownames  = FALSE
  )
```

This renders as an interactive HTML table with search, sort, and download — works in any self-contained `.html` or Shiny app.

> The file bw_assessment_eea_datahub_1990_2024_data.csv

## Key takeaways

::: {.incremental}
- **Copilot** = inline completion, fast, no project context
- **Claude Code** = agentic, reads files, iterates on errors
- **`btw`** = your live R session as an AI tool — describe only what's needed
- **`CLAUDE.md`** = free persistent project memory for Claude Code
- **`_quarto.yml`** = set your identity and style once, reuse forever
- **LM Studio** = same workflow, offline, weaker model
- **Git first** — always commit before an AI session
:::
